thread.title: Special Participation A: Perplexity Sonar on HW8

thread.document:
Executive Summary

I used Perplexity’s default LLM (as of Dec 2025) "Sonar" on the non-coding parts of Homework set 8 (Problems 1, 3, and 4). It answered almost all subparts correctly on the first try, including derivations for the convolution kernel, impulse-response interpretation, complexity comparisons, and the self-supervised linear purification / ridge-attention math. The main failure was the first attempt at the diagonal-plus-low-rank (DPLR) SSM kernel (Problem 1(f)): the model produced an incorrect, hand-wavy spectral argument with invented “perturbative terms,” but when I explicitly challenged its confidence, it produced a clean, correct eigen-decomposition-based derivation. When pushed, it was able to self-diagnose its previous mistakes, explicitly list what it had gotten wrong, and then re-derive the result more rigorously. The interaction felt less like getting final answers from an oracle and more like supervising a strong but occasionally overconfident collaborator who needs spot checks on nontrivial linear-algebra structure. Overall, for this session the LLM “one-shot” most sub-questions, but required human skepticism and targeted follow-up prompts to avoid accepting a superficially impressive but wrong derivation.

Setup and Strategy

Model and interface: Perplexity AI’s "Sonar" chat model (browser UI). The transcript in Problem 1_ SSM Convolution Kernel.md is essentially the raw LLM output, plus a short human challenge around Part (f).

Scope: I asked it to solve the non-coding parts of:

Problem 1: SSM convolution kernel (parts (a)–(f), including diagonal and DPLR structure and complexity).

Problem 3: Self-supervised linear purification / regularized encoder (SVD-based derivation and hyperparameter selection).

Problem 4: Ridge-attention questions (incremental means, ridge normal equations, complexity, Sherman–Morrison, causal ridge-attention, and whether gradients “flow” through λ).

Prompting style:

I usually gave it the math problem statement and let it answer in one shot.

I only intervened when something looked clearly suspicious, and prompted it with inquiries to help it self-diagnose its mistakes.

After catching an error, I explicitly asked it to critique its own previous answer and then provide a corrected derivation.

This setup was intentionally “light-touch”: I wanted to see how far it could get without heavy-handed scaffolding, and then whether human pressure could rescue it from a bad initial derivation.

Problem 1: SSM Convolution Kernel

Parts (a)–(e): One-Shot Success

(a) Convolution kernel derivation: It correctly unrolled the SSM, derived xk​=∑ℓ=0k−1​AℓBuk−1−ℓ​, substituted into yk​, and reindexed to identify K0​=D and Km​=CAm−1B for m≥1. This is the standard textbook result and matches the official structure.

(b) Concrete scalar and 2D examples:

Scalar case: It made a reasonable assumption about D (the problem text didn’t specify δ), explicitly stated the assumption, and produced a decaying geometric kernel consistent with α=0.8.

2D case: It correctly computed K1​,K2​,K3​ via CB,CAB,CA2B, carefully multiplying matrices and explaining that the decaying impulse response reflects stability.

Behavior: Good at routine linear algebra, explicit about missing details / assumptions rather than hallucinating them as facts.

(c) Convolution vs. direct recursion:

It correctly noted that direct recursion over time has a sequential dependency with O(L) critical path.

For convolution it emphasized tree-structured reductions leading to O(logL) critical path with enough parallelism.

The analysis leans more toward parallel runtime intuition than strict “total flops,” but is consistent and not obviously wrong.

(d) Kernel computation with matrix powers:

Naive strategy (O(Ln3)) and repeated squaring idea were both standard.

It mixed together “work” vs. “critical path” a bit, but the high-level story—use fast exponentiation and then apply CAm−1B—was sensible.

(e) Diagonal A:

It correctly recognized that diagonal A turns matrix powers into elementwise powers and collapses Km​ to a scalar sum ∑i​Ci​λim−1​Bi​.

Complexity dropped to O(Ln), which matches the intended diagonal-structure speedup.

For these parts, the LLM essentially “one-shot” the derivations and got both the algebra and the qualitative interpretations right. I did not have to intervene.

Part (f): DPLR – Failure, Then Recovery Under Pressure

This was the main point where the model did not one-shot the problem.

First attempt (incorrect / hand-wavy):

It tried to reason about A=I+pp⊤ via Sherman–Morrison and vague “perturbative terms,” writing expressions like

(I+pp⊤)m=I+(emlog(1+p⊤p/2)−1)⋅(perturbative terms)

and a generic Amv=v+p(p⊤v)⋅(correction term).

The derivation didn’t clearly exploit the spectrum (one eigenvalue 1+∥p∥2, others 1) and gave an inflated complexity claim O(n2+Ln) without a clean algorithm.

My reaction: This read like “mathy-sounding nonsense” rather than a precise argument. I explicitly asked if it was confident and pointed out that I believed the solution should look different.

Second attempt (corrected derivation after challenge):

When challenged, the model restarted from the eigenstructure:

Showed that A has eigenvalues λ1​=1+p⊤p along p and 1 on the orthogonal complement.

Constructed a unit eigenvector u1​=p/∥p∥ and wrote the projector decomposition
A=(I−u1​u1⊤​)+λ1​u1​u1⊤​.

Then correctly derived
Am=I+(λ1m​−1)u1​u1⊤​.

From there, it derived
Km​=CAm−1B=CB+(λ1m−1​−1)(Cu1​)(u1⊤​B),
giving a scalar-formula kernel and an essentially O(n+L) algorithm when precomputations are amortized.

It also wrote a self-critique section explicitly listing what it had gotten wrong in the earlier attempt (vague perturbative language, sloppy complexity, not fully reducing to scalars).

Behavioral takeaway:

Without pressure, it was content to give a plausible-sounding but wrong derivation.

With a short critical prompt (“Are you confident? I think this is wrong.”), it was capable of producing a mathematically clean, structurally correct solution that is actually better than the first.

This suggests that for subtle linear-algebra structure questions, the model is highly capable but needs an active, skeptical user to avoid “beautiful hallucinations.”

Problem 3: Self-Supervised Linear Purification

Here the model handled every subpart in one shot and aligned well with the standard ridge / SVD story.

(a)(i) & (a)(ii):

Correctly computed reconstruction and regularization losses for the identity vs. projection encoders on the given numeric matrix.

Solved for the threshold λ where one encoder becomes worse: 2λ>0.001+λ⇒λ>0.001.

(b)(i) & (b)(ii):

Derived the optimal encoder in the SVD basis, W^=Udiag(σj2​/(σj2​+λ))U⊤, by changing coordinates and decomposing the loss by singular directions.

This matches the standard “ridge shrinkage in the principal-component basis” result.

(c) Hyperparameter range:

Correctly turned the preservation/attenuation constraints into inequalities on σj2​/(σj2​+λ) and solved to get 1≤λ≤4, citing the right singular values.

Behaviorally, this part shows the model is very good at structured linear regression derivations: it recognizes SVD as the right tool, carries through the algebra cleanly, and keeps track of norms and Frobenius invariance without hallucinated side-conditions.

Problem 4: Ridge-Attention

For this problem, the model again answered each subpart in one shot and its reasoning matched what I would expect from a strong student solution.

(a) Incremental mean: Gave the standard m′=(mn+xn+1​)/(n+1) (and the equivalent incremental form m′=m+(xn+1​−m)/(n+1)).

(b) Ridge normal equations: Correctly decomposed A⊤A+λI as λI+∑xi​xi⊤​ and A⊤y=∑xi​yi​.

(c) Non-causal ridge-attention complexity: Focused on forming and inverting K⊤K+λI and obtained O(nd2) leading term, which is the standard complexity.

(d) Gradient flow: Identified that gradients propagate through keys, queries, and values, but not typically through λ in standard setups.

(e) Sherman–Morrison cost: Broke down the matrix–vector and rank-1 updates to get O(d2) per update, which is correct.

(f) Causal ridge-attention: Wrote a plausible online algorithm using Sherman–Morrison to update the inverse and maintain a W matrix, with per-step O(d2) cost and total O(nd2). The structure matches the intended dynamic-programming intuition.

(g) Attention weights: Expressed the weights via the ridge coefficients and contrasted them with softmax attention (unconstrained, can be negative, don’t sum to 1).

Extra discussion: “Can gradients flow through λ?”

Here the model went beyond the likely intended scope of the homework and gave a long answer splitting “mathematically yes, practically no.”

Mathematically, it argued (correctly) that autograd can differentiate through matrix inverses via implicit differentiation, and even wrote the derivative formula.

Practically, it concluded that we shouldn’t treat λ as a learnable parameter for stability and regularization reasons, and guessed that the problem likely expects “no” as the conceptual answer.

This is a case where the LLM is technically correct but may overcomplicate what the assignment likely wanted (“λ is a hyperparameter, not a learned parameter”).

This section illustrates a pattern: the model is capable of sophisticated meta-reasoning, but it may miscalibrate what level of nuance is appropriate for a homework answer vs. a research discussion.

Takeaways and Recommendations

As a homework aid:

This LLM is very effective at deriving standard linear-algebra results and giving clear, step-by-step explanations.

For most subparts, I could have copied the answers with only minimal editing.

However, treating it as an infallible oracle would have led me to accept a wrong DPLR derivation, which is exactly the kind of subtle structural question that’s exam-relevant.

Best practices for using it:

Use it as a co-author for derivations: let it propose a solution, but then read critically and ask “Does this really use the structure the problem is hinting at?”

For tricky structural or complexity questions, plan to challenge its first answer and ask it to re-derive more cleanly or justify every step.

Consider asking it to explicitly list what assumptions it is making and what might fail.

Bottom line:

In this interaction, the LLM could essentially solve all non-coding parts of the assignment with high accuracy, but it still needed human mathematical judgment to catch a key mistake and to calibrate how much nuance is appropriate for a course setting.

If used thoughtfully and skeptically, it is a very strong tool for both checking work and deepening understanding; if used uncritically, it can quietly introduce subtle but important errors in exactly the kinds of problems that are hardest to catch by inspection.
